passage:
In the college library's group-study room, Ishita dropped her bag on the table. "Pranav, you vanished for four days. The presentation is tomorrow."
Pranav winced. In psych elective they had just done attachment styles, and a classmate had joked, "Avoidant, so not my fault!" It would be easy to say that now.
"I know. When our group chat got tense, I did my usual thing and went quiet. With my cousins I don't, but under pressure I do. That explains it. It doesn't excuse it." He opened his laptop. "My four slides are done, and I'll do the conclusion too. Next time I'll say I need an hour instead of disappearing."
Ishita sat down. "Okay. Show me the slides."

qa.q: How long had Pranav been missing from the group?
qa.a: He vanished for four days.

qa.q: Why did Pranav wince when Ishita spoke?
qa.a: He felt guilty, knowing he had let the group down right before the presentation.

qa.q: What choice did Pranav make instead of hiding behind a label?
qa.a: He explained his tendency to go quiet under pressure but said it was no excuse, finished his slides, took on the conclusion and promised to ask for an hour next time.

qa.q: How might Ishita have reacted if Pranav had said "Avoidant, not my fault"?
qa.a: She would probably have been more frustrated, since the label would dodge responsibility for the missing work.

grounding: A student uses the idea of attachment style to understand his withdrawal, notes it varies by setting, and still takes responsibility.

passage:
Dear Harsha,
After our fight on Saturday you said, "That's just my anxious attachment, you knew that when we started." I've been thinking about it all week.
I read the same book you did, and I think it's useful. It helps me see why a late reply hits you so hard, and why I go stiff when you get upset. But I don't think either of us is only a type. You're calm as anything with your students at the tuition centre. I'm not distant with my sister.
So can we use it as a map, not a verdict? I'll own that I went quiet for a whole day. Can you own the twelve messages?
I want to keep going. Just with both of us taking our share.
Tejas

qa.q: Where is Harsha calm with students?
qa.a: At the tuition centre.

qa.q: What was Tejas worried about after Harsha pointed to attachment style?
qa.a: Tejas worried the label was being used as a verdict and an excuse, so neither of them would take responsibility.

qa.q: What turning point does Tejas propose in the letter?
qa.a: Tejas suggests treating attachment styles as a map rather than a verdict, owning a day of silence and asking Harsha to own the twelve messages.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel reading "Can you own the twelve messages?"
qa.a: Harsha may feel stung at first but also respected, since Tejas owns a share first and says the relationship is worth continuing.

grounding: A young adult writes that attachment styles vary with context and help explain reactions but do not excuse behaviour on either side.

passage: For a while I had the perfect excuse. I'd read one article and decided: I'm Karthik, and I'm avoidant. So when my friend Pankaj's father was in hospital and I didn't call for a week, I told myself, that's just my attachment style. Pankaj didn't buy it. He said, "You're not a label. You're my friend who went missing." That hit hard. Now I think of it more like weather: I do pull back when things get heavy, especially with family stuff, less with teammates. Knowing that helps me catch it. It doesn't let me off. So I called him, apologised without the jargon, and drove him to the hospital on Sunday.

qa.q: What did Karthik do on Sunday?
qa.a: Drove Pankaj to the hospital.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel when Pankaj said "You're my friend who went missing"?
qa.a: Karthik felt stung and ashamed, realising the label had been used as an excuse.

qa.q: What is the wiser way Karthik now uses the idea of attachment style?
qa.a: As a tendency that helps notice when pulling back starts, while still taking responsibility and showing up.

qa.q: How did Pankaj experience Karthik's week of silence?
qa.a: Pankaj felt let down by a missing friend while his father was in hospital, and would not accept the label as an excuse.

grounding: Shows a young adult who stops using an attachment label as an excuse and treats it as a tendency while taking responsibility.

passage: I'm Chetan, Bhavna's classmate on the design course, and I've watched her change this year. In first year, if her boyfriend didn't text back, she'd tell us, "I'm anxiously attached, I can't help it," and send twenty messages. This term something shifted. I overheard her in the canteen telling a friend, "Yeah, I lean anxious, mostly with him, not with you lot. But that's not his job to fix." During our group critique she put her phone in her bag and didn't touch it for an hour. When she snapped at a junior over a model, she went back and apologised. I don't know what goes on inside her head. But she seems to use the words to understand herself, not to hide.

qa.q: How long did Bhavna leave her phone in her bag during the critique?
qa.a: For an hour.

qa.q: What might Bhavna be feeling when she says "that's not his job to fix"?
qa.a: She seems more settled and responsible, less panicked, owning her anxious tendency instead of blaming it.

qa.q: What does Bhavna do that shows she takes responsibility for her behaviour?
qa.a: She puts the phone away during the critique and goes back to apologise after snapping at a junior.

qa.q: How does Chetan see the change in Bhavna?
qa.a: Chetan notices she now uses the words to understand herself rather than as an excuse, while admitting not knowing her inner thoughts.

grounding: Shows through a classmate's eyes a person treating attachment style as a context-dependent tendency, not an excuse.

passage:
Week one, a Monday: When Maria asked why Ayesha had ignored her texts all weekend, Ayesha shrugged. "I'm avoidant. It's how I'm wired." Maria went quiet and left for class.
Week three, a Thursday: Ayesha noticed she answered her cricket teammates within minutes but froze when her roommate wrote anything personal. So it wasn't everyone, all the time.
Week four, a Sunday: She knocked on Maria's door. "I used that word like a shield. I do pull away when things get personal, but ignoring you was my choice, and it was unkind. I'm sorry." Maria moved her laundry off the bed so Ayesha could sit.

qa.q: How quickly did Ayesha answer her cricket teammates?
qa.a: Within minutes.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel when she knocked on Maria's door?
qa.a: She seemed humbled and sorry, ready to own that ignoring Maria was her choice.

qa.q: What did Ayesha notice that changed how she saw the label?
qa.a: That she only froze with personal messages, so the tendency depended on context rather than being fixed.

qa.q: How does Maria show her response to the apology?
qa.a: She moves her laundry so Ayesha can sit, showing she is willing to reconnect.

grounding: Shows across weeks a young adult moving from using an attachment label as an excuse to seeing it as a tendency and taking responsibility.

passage:
Nirmala, you keep saying "I'm just avoidant, that's how I am." Let your Shalini Aunty tell you something.
At twenty, I read an article about attachment styles and decided I was "avoidant". It felt like a relief, like a name for everything. When my friend Rupa was upset that I ignored her calls for a week, I said, "Sorry, that's my style." She stared at me and said, "Your style hurt me."
That stung. I went home and thought about it. With my grandmother I wasn't avoidant at all; I called her every day. With Rupa I pulled back only when she needed me.
So the label wasn't who I was. It helped me see why I pulled away. But I still owed Rupa an apology, and I gave her one, properly, at her doorstep, with her favourite sweets.
Use the idea to understand yourself, beta. Not as an excuse.

qa.q: Who did young Shalini call every day?
qa.a: Her grandmother.

qa.q: How did young Shalini feel when Rupa said "Your style hurt me"?
qa.a: She felt stung and ashamed, which made her go home and rethink using the label.

qa.q: What choice did young Shalini make after Rupa's words, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She took responsibility and apologised properly at Rupa's doorstep, instead of hiding behind the label.

qa.q: How did Rupa see the "that's my style" excuse?
qa.a: Rupa saw it as brushing off her hurt; a label didn't make being ignored for a week feel any better to her.

grounding: Shows an aunt recalling how she learned that an attachment style is a context-dependent tendency, not an identity or excuse, and still owned her behaviour.
